header:
Date: 2025-11-06
Time: 15:00 - 15:52 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Murdock (Redwood AE), Sara Lin (Redwood SE), Daniel Park (Redwood), Dr. Priya Nair (CISO, Montclair Health), Tom Wagner (Infra Lead), Elena Ruiz (Compliance), Samir Patel (App Security)
Recording: Yes
Deck: shared (link placeholder)
topics: Data residency and region pinning (EU-only processing)
Cross-border egress controls and contractual commitments

Subprocessor disclosure and flow chart (data path)
Audit logs retention, export to customer SIEM, and tamper-evidence
SOC 2 / ISO alignment and contract language for egress restrictions
transcript:
[00:00] Alex (AE): Okay, welcome everyone, thanks for making time. We're here to go through Montclair's data egress and KMS questions, yeah. I'll kick off with a quick agenda — region pinning, subprocessor flows, and then Sara will go deeper on key management.
[00:20] Dr. Priya: Thanks Alex. Our big ask is straightforward — PHI and patient-facing transcripts must stay in the EU datacenter footprint, no copies leaving for processing in the US without explicit authorization. We also need detection and contractual recourse if any routing crosses borders.
[00:38] Alex: Totally understood. Sara, quick intro?
[00:42] Sara (SE): Hey all — I'm Sara, I own infra and security design for customers doing EU-only requirements. Quick note, I may mangle acronyms occasionally, so feel free to jump in.
[00:52] [02:05] Tom (Infra): A practical question: is region pinning a hard tenancy guarantee or request routing? We need no chance of failover to US for these tenant IDs.
[02:22] Sara: Good question. We support strict region affinity/pinning at the tenant level. For Dedicated and Private deployments it's deterministic — you control where compute runs. For Hosted, we offer region pinning plus policy-based routing; we can add hard egress guards to abort requests destined for other regions. There are tradeoffs for availability.
[02:44] Dr. Priya: We care more about sovereignty and auditability than 99.99% availability, so availability tradeoffs are acceptable if we have guarantees. Also, we're very concerned about temporary cache replication (prefix/KV cache). How is that handled?
[03:03] Sara: We have explicit controls: KV cache and prefix cache for pinned tenants can be scoped to region. By default in Hosted mode caches are region-local; but there are edge cases during burst or failover where cache state could be replicated to a standby region — we can disable cross-region replication for pinned tenants.
[03:25] Samir (App Security): You said "edge cases" — can you describe those and how they are logged?
[03:31] Sara: Sure. Example: if a node in Region EU-West fails and autoscaling triggers capacity in EU-Central we clone runtime state within EU. The "edge case" we'd worry about is if primary capacity is exhausted and we attempt a cross-region fallback to US. That fallback is a policy we can turn off. If it's off, requests will queue or error rather than cross borders. We also emit an egress event to audit logs.
[03:54] [05:12] Elena (Compliance): What about subprocessors? We need a full chain: who operates the network, who operates storage, any analytics vendors.
[05:20] Alex: We'll share the subprocessor inventory. High level: cloud infra provider (name masked in recording), observability provider, optional CDNs for static assets. For EU-pinned tenants we limit subprocessors to EU-region equivalents where possible.
[05:36] Dr. Priya: We need contractual SCCs and also question about subcontractor tiers. If a subprocessors' provider has US staff who can access, does that count as cross-border?
[05:48] Daniel (Redwood): Access controls are role-bound. Most subcontractors have admin panels accessible from multiple geos but admin access doesn't imply data egress — data plane stays in region. However, we do have to be explicit about access for maintenance and emergency.
[06:05] Tom: Are logs redacted or do audit logs contain payloads? We can't have PHI in audit trail stored outside the region.
[06:12] Sara: Audit logs are configurable. For EU-pinned tenants we offer PII/PHI scrubbing in logs and the option to export raw logs into the customer's own SIEM in-region. The default aggregated metrics we keep for platform health are anonymized and do not include user content.
[06:36] [07:45] Samir: KMS — what's the HSM story? Can you do customer-managed keys that never leave our HSM? We need crypto such that Redwood cannot decrypt customer data without a split key.
[07:55] Sara: We support several models: (1) Redwood-managed KMS in-region, (2) customer-managed keys in their cloud KMS integrated via Bring Your Own Key (BYOK), (3) key-splitting where a portion of an encryption key is held by the customer (we call it split-key) and Redwood holds the rest, requiring both halves to unwrap. For the strongest guarantee we recommend customer KMS with HSM-backed keys plus a split-key arrangement. Note: split-key requires integration work and some latency impact.
[08:27] Dr. Priya: Can you detail the split key workflow? For encryption at rest and in-flight — do you rewrap tokens on every inference request?
[08:34] Sara: Short answer: we keep long-lived data encrypted at rest with a master key (CMK). For ephemeral per-request material (like session envelopes) we do on-demand key unwrapping. With split key, the CMK is derived such that a customer-held fragment is required to perform unwrap. That fragment is never transmitted to Redwood. We do a remote attestation handshake to verify the customer fragment is present. There is a short-lived cache of unwrapped envelopes in memory only, and we never persist unwrapped keys to disk.
[09:10] [10:30] Dr. Priya: Legal will ask about lawful interception and subpoenas. If a government in the EU requests data, what's the disclosure path? We need to ensure we are notified and there's a minimum process.
[10:42] Alex: We include the standard notification clause where allowed by law — we notify customers unless prohibited. For EU regions, we route legal requests through our legal team and provide transparency reporting. For hosted customers with EU-only controls, we will push back and require jurisdictional grounding before any cross-border transfer.
[10:59] Tom: Hypothetical: an infra incident requires emergency cross-region failover and a US engineer performs troubleshooting. Does that create a path for PHI to be exposed?
[11:12] Sara: Emergency operations can be tightly scoped. We offer a "narrowed access window" model: read-only debug snapshots can be created and it's possible to require customer approval or a joint break-glass with audit records. Also, snapshots can be scrubbed of PHI before viewing. This is configurable per contract.
[11:38] [13:10] Elena: About audit logs retention — what's the default retention of request logs and how long are they stored in raw form?
[13:18] Sara: Default platform logs are 90 days for full verbose logs, 365 days for aggregated metrics. For EU-pinned customers we can shorten or move raw logs into the customer's retention store in-region, and configure redaction to remove content.
[13:34] Dr. Priya: That sounds promising. We also want machine-readable proof that region pinning was honored per request in case of audit. Do you emit per-request region metadata?
[13:45] Sara: Yes — each request includes a region tag and a routing decision record. Those are stored in the audit log and are exportable. We can also sign routing records with platform key to create tamper-proof evidence. There is a small implementation lead to enable signed routing records.
[14:07] [15:00] Samir: On SOC 2 and ISO, can you share the latest report and scope? We specifically want controls around logical access, change mgmt, and vendor management.
[15:09] Alex: We'll provide the SOC 2 Type II report and current ISO attestations. The reports include control descriptions; note that detailed evidence often requires an NDA or an in-contract right to audit.
[15:20] Elena: We'll need the artifact and also suggested contract language that ties those controls to breach remedies.
[15:27] [16:40] Tom: Network egress — can you put a denial rule so that any outbound traffic to non-EU public IPs from the pinned tenant is blocked at L3?
[16:49] Daniel: At the host and VPC level we can implement deny-lists for egress and restrict NAT gateways. For Hosted tenants we can enforce network policies and have a managed egress firewall. If Private deployment, you manage it directly. We can add a contract SLA that any attempted non-EU egress triggers an alert and is blocked.
[17:12] [18:30] Dr. Priya: About subprocessors — we need a downstream flow diagram: who touches the data, for what purpose, and where they are located. Can you produce that?
[18:40] Alex: Yes, action item for us to produce a data flow diagram that lists each subprocessor and their country. We will mark EU-only subprocessors for the pinned tenant.
[18:50] [20:05] Samir: Regarding encryption in transit — do you support mutual TLS with client certs for internal components? We need to ensure east-west traffic inside the platform is authenticated and encrypted.
[20:15] Sara: All internal service-to-service traffic uses mTLS within our service mesh. For customer-facing endpoints we support mTLS and client certs if customers want to lock to their own certs.
[20:30] Tom: One concern: logs forwarded to our SIEM — is that push or pull? We prefer push via an outbox in-region rather than us having to pull data across the wire.
[20:38] Sara: We support both. For EU-pinned customers we can push logs via a secure, encrypted stream to a customer-managed SIEM connector inside EU.
[20:47] [22:10] Dr. Priya: On key rotation — how often are platform keys rotated and what is the impact on session state?
[22:18] Sara: Platform master keys rotate per our key policy quarterly; customers with BYOK control rotation cadence. Rotation is designed to be non-disruptive; we rewrap data keys and keep old keys available for unwrap until all rewrapping completes. There are transient CPU costs but not downtime.
[22:36] [24:05] Elena: A slightly different question: can Redwood provide a contractual prohibition on transferring data to countries on our restricted list unless we explicitly allow?
[24:15] Alex: Yes, we can add explicit geography clauses to the contract — list-based prohibitions are common. We'll follow up with suggested language.
[24:25] [25:50] Samir: For the split-key model, who performs attestation of the remote fragment? We need cryptographic proof the fragment is present and hasn't been substituted.
[25:58] Sara: We use remote attestation patterns similar to challenge-response; the customer fragment signs a nonce and Redwood verifies the signature during unwrap. We can combine this with HSM-backed attestation if the customer's KMS supports it. We'll include a more detailed diagram in the SE deep dive.
[26:22] [28:05] Tom: Performance note: if every request requires a round-trip to the customer KMS for attestation, latency will spike. Any mitigations?
[28:14] Sara: Right — we normally cache attestation tokens for a short window and do pre-warming for high-throughput workloads, and we recommend colocating KMS in the same region. Also, we can use short-lived session keys derived after attestation to avoid per-request KMS calls. This is a standard tradeoff between security and latency.
[28:40] [30:00] Dr. Priya: Are you able to provide sample evidence for a third-party audit that region pinning has been enforced over a 6-month window?
[30:09] Alex: We can produce routing logs and signed routing records for any timeframe within our retention window, assuming we haven't been asked to redact them. For longer retention we can export to the customer's archive. We'll generate a sample pack.
[30:23] [31:45] Elena: Is there an option for a full on-prem Private deployment? We'd like to consider that for highest assurance.
[31:55] Sara: Yes. Private on-prem or VPC-hosted deployment gives you maximum control — you run the inference runtime in your environment, Redwood provides control plane components optionally via a managed channel. That eliminates cross-border concerns but increases integration effort and support model.
[32:14] Tom: How long is Redwood's support window for on-prem versions? Patching cadence?
[32:20] Daniel: We maintain regular patch releases and backport critical security fixes for the supported lifecycle in the contract — typically 12 months for minor older versions unless extended in enterprise SLAs.
[32:34] [34:00] Samir: A compliance nit: we need to ensure staff with access to customer data are bound by EU data processing agreements and local screening — do you have policies for staff location limits?
[34:12] Alex: Yes, for EU-pinned contracts we can require that only EU-based operations staff have access, or we can require that any non-EU access be subject to additional controls and approval. We'll enumerate options in the subprocessor and access policy doc.
[34:32] [36:05] Dr. Priya: About the fail-open vs fail-close behavior — we want fail-close by default on region mismatch. Does Redwood support making "fail-open" an explicit opt-in?
[36:20] Sara: Yes — default is configurable per tenant. For Montclair we'd set fail-close: if routing would cross region, reject and emit alert. We can also add an emergency manual override under a break-glass with recorded approvals.
[36:38] [38:10] Tom: On multi-tenant isolation, are there dedicated GPU pools for EU-pinned customers or do you mix with other tenants?
[38:20] Daniel: Both options exist. For Hosted we have multi-tenant pools with strong isolation; for Dedicated you get reserved GPU capacity. For the strictest isolation, Dedicated or Private deployments are recommended.
[38:36] [40:00] Elena: Can you sign a clause saying you'll notify us within X hours of any region policy violation? What is realistic?
[40:08] Alex: We can commit to a 24-hour notification window for region policy violations, and real-time alerts as they occur. For high-severity incidents we do immediate paging. We'll map notification SLAs in the contract.
[40:20] [42:00] Dr. Priya: A question from legal: if a subprocessor changes its location, how will we be notified?
[42:08] Alex: We will provide 30-day notice for subprocessor location changes, and customers can object and require migration or termination for their data. Standard practice is to allow a migration window.
[42:20] [44:15] Samir: Any third-party penetration test results we can see?
[44:23] Alex: We'll include summary findings and remediation evidence; detailed reports usually require NDA. We'll attach summary to the next email.
[44:34] [46:00] Sara: Quick recap from SE side — technical options we recommend: BYOK + split-key + HSM for full sovereignty; enforce fail-close routing; configure log push to customer SIEM in EU; disable any cross-region cache replication for pinned tenants; provide signed routing evidence.
[46:18] Elena: That's the core asks. Also, list of subprocessors and the contract language.
[46:26] Alex: Perfect. Next steps: we'll send SOC2 report and subprocessor inventory, Sara will follow up with deep-dive on KMS and key-split architecture, and we can schedule the pilot for EU-pinned tenant.
[46:40] [48:50] Tom: One last practical — cost impact? Anything we should plan for?
[48:58] Sara: Key-splitting and HSM add modest per-request latency and some additional monthly fees for HSM and dedicated capacity if you choose Dedicated or Private. We'll include a cost delta in the pilot proposal.
[49:14] Dr. Priya: OK thanks. Any final thoughts?
[49:18] Alex: Thanks everyone; we'll follow up with artifacts and proposed contract language.
[49:30] [51:45] Elena: Thanks all.
[51:48] Alex: Meeting adjourned.
